title: 01. Fundamentals: Creating Strings — All Ways
summary: Python provides multiple ways to create strings. Understanding all of them helps you write cleaner code.
objectives: Raw string cannot END with odd number of backslashes

sections.title: CONCEPT EXPLANATION
sections.body:
Python provides multiple ways to create strings. Understanding all of them helps you write cleaner code.

### All Creation Methods:

```python
# 1. Single quotes — most common for simple strings
name = 'Alice'

# 2. Double quotes — use when string contains single quote
msg = "It's a beautiful day"

# 3. Triple single quotes — multiline, preserves formatting
poem = '''Roses are red,
Violets are blue'''

# 4. Triple double quotes — often used for docstrings
doc = """This function does
something important."""

# 5. Raw strings (r"") — backslash NOT treated as escape
path = r"C:\Users\Veerababu\Documents"

# 6. Byte strings (b"") — for bytes, not text
data = b"Hello bytes"

# 7. f-strings — embedded expressions (Python 3.6+)
age = 26
greeting = f"I am {age} years old"

# 8. str() constructor — convert other types
num_str = str(42)
bool_str = str(True)
```

### ⚠️ Escape Characters — Critical to Know!

| Escape | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `\n` | Newline | `"Line1\nLine2"` |
| `\t` | Tab | `"Col1\tCol2"` |
| `\\` | Literal backslash | `"C:\\path"` |
| `\'` | Literal single quote | `'It\'s fine'` |
| `\"` | Literal double quote | `"He said \"Hi\""` |
| `\r` | Carriage return | used in Windows files |
| `\0` | Null character | rare, special use |
| `\uXXXX` | Unicode character | `"\u0041"` = "A" |

sections.title: 5 EXAMPLES
sections.body:
**What this code covers** - It's a "complex" string - Dear {name}, - SELECT u.name, u.email, o.total FROM users u JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id WHERE u.active = TRUE AND o.date >= '2026-01-01' ORDER BY o.total DESC… - Hello, {name}! - Single quotes — simple strings - Double quotes — when content has apostrophes - Mixing — avoid escape characters - When you need BOTH — use triple quotes or escape ### Example 1: Quote Types and When to Use Each ```python # Single quotes — simple strings product = 'Laptop' city = 'Hyderabad' # Double quotes — when content has apostrophes message = "It's a great day to learn Python!" quote = "She said, 'Hello there!'" # Mixing — avoid escape characters hard_way = 'It\'s Python' # Need to escape easy_way = "It's Python" # No escape needed! hard_way2 = "She said \"Hi\"" # Need to escape easy_way2 = 'She said "Hi"' # No escape needed! print(message) print(quote) print(easy_way) print(easy_way2) # When you need BOTH — use triple quotes or escape both = """It's a "complex" string""" print(both) # It's a "complex" string ``` ### Example 2: Raw Strings — Windows Paths and Regex ```python # ❌ WITHOUT raw string — backslash causes issues # \n = newline, \t = tab, \U = Unicode escape! bad_path = "C:\new_folder\test_file\Users" print(bad_path) # WRONG! \n and \t are escape sequences! # ✅ WITH raw string — backslash is literal good_path = r"C:\new_folder\test_file\Users" print(good_path) # C:\new_folder\test_file\Users ✅ # Alternative with double backslash also_good = "C:\\new_folder\\test_file\\Users" print(also_good) # Same result # Raw strings in regex patterns (covered in Chapter 13) import re # Without raw string — need double backslash pattern1 = "\\d+" # matches digits # With raw string — cleaner! pattern2 = r"\d+" # Same thing, much cleaner! ``` # ⚠️ Raw string cannot END with odd number of backslashes # r"path\" ← SyntaxError! # r"path\\" ← OK (two backslashes) ``` ``` ### Example 3: Multiline Strings — Triple Quotes ```python # Multiline string — preserves newlines and indentation email_template = """ Dear {name}, Thank you for registering with us. Your account details: Username: {username} Email: {email} Please verify your email within 24 hours. Best regards, The Support Team """ # Use it as a template filled = email_template.format( name="Veerababu Kumar", username="veerababu74", email="veera@example.com" ) print(filled) # SQL queries — multiline for readability sql_query = """ SELECT u.name, u.email, o.total FROM users u JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id WHERE u.active = TRUE AND o.date >= '2026-01-01' ORDER BY o.total DESC LIMIT 10 """ print("SQL Query ready!") # HTML template html = """

Hello, {name}!

""".format(name="World") ``` ### Example 4: Escape Sequences in Practice ```python # Common escape sequences you'll actually use # \n — newline (most common) address = "123 Main Street\nHyderabad, Telangana\nIndia - 500001" print(address) # 123 Main Street # Hyderabad, Telangana # India - 500001 # \t — tab (for formatting) report_row = "Alice\t\t85000\t\tEngineering" print(report_row) # Alice 85000 Engineering # \\ — literal backslash windows_path = "C:\\Users\\Veerababu\\Documents" print(windows_path) # C:\Users\Veerababu\Documents # \' and \" in strings print('It\'s working!') # It's working! print("He said \"Hello\"") # He said "Hello" # \u — Unicode characters rupee = "\u20B9" # ₹ Indian Rupee symbol heart = "\u2764" # ❤ Heart print(f"Price: {rupee}55,000") # Price: ₹55,000 # chr() and ord() — convert between char and code print(ord('A')) # 65 print(chr(65)) # A print(chr(0x20B9)) # ₹ ``` ### Example 5: String Creation from Other Types ```python # str() — universal converter print(str(42)) # "42" print(str(3.14)) # "3.14" print(str(True)) # "True" print(str(False)) # "False" print(str(None)) # "None" print(str([1, 2, 3])) # "[1, 2, 3]" print(str({"a": 1})) # "{'a': 1}" # Format numbers as strings with specific representation print(f"{255:b}") # 11111111 — binary print(f"{255:o}") # 377 — octal print(f"{255:x}") # ff — hex lowercase print(f"{255:X}") # FF — hex uppercase print(f"{3.14159:.2f}") # 3.14 — 2 decimal places print(f"{1000000:,}") # 1,000,000 — with commas print(f"{0.75:.1%}") # 75.0% — percentage # Build string from character codes codes = [72, 101, 108, 108, 111] word = ''.join(chr(c) for c in codes) print(word) # Hello # Repeat a string line = "-" * 40 print(line) # ---------------------------------------- ```
